title: The Triumph of Conservatism
summary: Richard Nixon won the White House on a backlash against 1960s upheaval, yet he governed pragmatically, expanding the Great Society he inherited: his administration created the EPA and OSHA, broadened food stamps, indexed Social Security, and even proposed a guaranteed minimum income. Abroad, Nixon and Henry Kissinger practiced 'realist' diplomacy, opening relations with communist China in 1972 and signing the SALT arms-control agreements with the Soviets, launching an era of détente. But Vietnam dragged on—the Cambodia invasion of 1970 triggered killings at Kent State, and the Pentagon Papers exposed decades of official deception—until the 1973 Paris accords ended U.S. involvement. Nixon's obsession with enemies produced the Watergate break-in and cover-up, and in August 1974 he became the first president to resign, deepening public distrust already fed by revelations of CIA and FBI abuses.

The 1970s also ended the postwar economic golden age. The 1973 Arab oil embargo quadrupled energy prices, and 'stagflation'—stagnant growth combined with high inflation—defied liberal remedies. Deindustrialization moved manufacturing jobs to the low-wage Sunbelt and overseas, real wages began a long decline, and unions weakened. Gerald Ford's presidency produced little beyond the Helsinki Accords, while Jimmy Carter, elected as a post-Watergate outsider in 1976, made human rights central to foreign policy and brokered the Camp David peace between Egypt and Israel. But Three Mile Island, a second oil shock, the Iranian hostage crisis, and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan made Carter appear helpless.

These dislocations fueled a conservative movement uniting neoconservative intellectuals, the evangelical Religious Right, anti-tax rebels behind California's Proposition 13, Sunbelt suburbanites, and opponents of the ERA and abortion. Ronald Reagan harnessed this coalition in 1980, promising to restore American strength and making 'freedom' the rallying cry of the right. His supply-side tax cuts, deregulation, and firing of striking air traffic controllers curbed inflation and spurred growth, but inequality widened and the national debt tripled. After a massive military buildup and the Iran-Contra scandal, Reagan surprised critics by negotiating historic arms reductions with Mikhail Gorbachev, leaving office with the Cold War thawing and conservatism dominant.
big_ideas: Nixon pursued centrist domestic policies—creating the EPA and expanding welfare programs—while his foreign policy of détente reoriented the Cold War through openings to China and the Soviet Union.
Vietnam and Watergate together shattered Americans' trust in the federal government, strengthening the conservative argument that Washington's power should be limited.
The 1970s economy of oil shocks, stagflation, and deindustrialization ended postwar prosperity, began a long decline in real wages, and shifted population and power to the Sunbelt.
A new conservative coalition—neoconservatives, the Religious Right, tax rebels, and 'family values' activists—mobilized against the rights revolution, defeating the ERA and contesting abortion.
Reagan's 1980 victory brought supply-side economics, deregulation, and anti-union policies that revived growth but sharply increased inequality and federal deficits.
Reagan revived Cold War confrontation and covert intervention abroad, producing the Iran-Contra scandal, yet his later diplomacy with Gorbachev dramatically eased superpower tensions.
By 1988 conservatism had captured the language of freedom and set the terms of national politics for both parties.

key_terms.def: Nixon-era policy of easing tensions with the Soviet Union and China, replacing rigid Cold War hostility with negotiation, trade, and arms control.
The 1972 Strategic Arms Limitation Treaty produced by U.S.-Soviet talks, which capped nuclear missile arsenals and, with the ABM Treaty, barred missile-defense systems.

A secret Defense Department history of the Vietnam War leaked by Daniel Ellsberg and published in 1971, revealing that successive presidents had misled the public; the Supreme Court refused to block publication.
A 1973 law requiring congressional approval for sending U.S. troops abroad, the strongest legislative check on presidential war-making in American history.
The 1968 killing of hundreds of Vietnamese civilians by American troops; its exposure in 1969 deepened public disillusionment with the war.

The scandal that began with a 1972 break-in at Democratic headquarters by operatives tied to Nixon's reelection campaign; the cover-up, revealed through tapes and hearings, forced Nixon's resignation in 1974.
The 1973 cutoff of petroleum exports by Arab OPEC states in retaliation for Western support of Israel; it caused gas shortages, soaring prices, and global recession.
The 1970s combination of slow economic growth, high unemployment, and high inflation that discredited traditional liberal economic management.
The late-twentieth-century collapse of manufacturing in older industrial regions as companies automated and shifted production to the low-wage South, West, and overseas.
The band of southern and western states that gained population, jobs, and political clout in the postwar decades, becoming a stronghold of modern conservatism.

The 1978 Supreme Court decision striking down fixed racial quotas in university admissions while permitting race to count as one factor among many; it remains the touchstone for affirmative action law.
The 1978 peace framework between Egypt and Israel personally brokered by President Carter, a landmark of his human-rights-centered diplomacy.
Jerry Falwell's 1979 organization of the Religious Right, which mobilized evangelical Christians behind 'pro-family' conservative candidates and causes.
California's 1978 voter initiative freezing property taxes, the signal victory of a national tax revolt that fed conservative politics.

Reagan's supply-side program of deep tax cuts for businesses and the wealthy, deregulation, and tight money; it tamed inflation and spurred growth but tripled the national debt and widened inequality.
The Reagan administration scandal in which officials secretly sold arms to Iran and illegally funneled the proceeds to Nicaraguan Contra rebels in defiance of a congressional ban.

timeline.event: Nixon orders the invasion of Cambodia; National Guardsmen kill four students at Kent State.
Pentagon Papers published; Nixon takes the United States off the gold standard.
Nixon visits China and signs SALT in Moscow; Congress passes Title IX and sends the ERA to the states; Watergate break-in occurs.
Paris Peace Accords end U.S. combat in Vietnam; Arab oil embargo begins; Congress passes the War Powers Act.
Facing impeachment over Watergate, Nixon resigns; Gerald Ford becomes president and pardons him.
South Vietnam falls to the North; the Helsinki Accords are signed.
Jimmy Carter, campaigning as an outsider, narrowly defeats Ford.
Proposition 13 passes in California; Bakke decision limits affirmative action quotas; Camp David Accords reached.
Three Mile Island accident; Iranian revolutionaries seize American hostages; Moral Majority founded; Soviets invade Afghanistan.
Ronald Reagan defeats Carter, launching the Reagan Revolution.
Reagan wins major tax cuts and fires 13,000 striking air traffic controllers.
Iran-Contra hearings expose illegal arms deals; Reagan and Gorbachev agree to eliminate intermediate-range nuclear missiles.

themes: Politics and power: Watergate and Vietnam eroded faith in government, and a rising conservative coalition redefined freedom as limited government, low taxes, and traditional values.
Work, exchange, and technology: Oil shocks, stagflation, and deindustrialization ended the postwar boom, weakened unions, and began a lasting decline in real wages for ordinary workers.
America in the world: Policy swung from Nixon's détente to Carter's human-rights diplomacy to Reagan's renewed Cold War—and finally to arms-reduction breakthroughs with Gorbachev.
Geography and environment: Population and industry flowed to the Sunbelt, while environmental regulation expanded under Nixon and then sparked western resistance in the Sagebrush Rebellion.
American identity: Battles over the ERA, abortion, busing, and affirmative action revealed deep divisions over gender roles, race, and the meaning of equality.
